summary: Describes authentication mechanisms for the IMAP4 AUTHENTICATE command, which identifies a user to the server and can negotiate protection for later traffic. The mechanisms covered include Kerberos, GSSAPI and S/KEY.

eli5.summary: Different secret handshakes a mail program can use to prove who you are before it opens your mailbox.

questions: how does kerberos work with imap
subtitle: Three ways an IMAP4 client can prove who it is: Kerberos v4, GSSAPI and S/Key.

tldr.problem: The IMAP4 AUTHENTICATE command needs concrete mechanisms for identifying a user to the server and, optionally, agreeing on protection for the rest of the session.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three mechanisms, KERBEROS_V4, GSSAPI and SKEY, each as a sequence of 'ready' responses and client replies carrying tickets, tokens or one-time passwords.
tldr.outcome: Kerberos and GSSAPI can negotiate integrity or privacy protection; S/Key gives one-time-password login with no protection mechanisms.

today: RFC 1731 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It extends the AUTHENTICATE command of RFC 1730.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Internet Message Access Protocol version 4 (RFC 1730) has an AUTHENTICATE command. It identifies and authenticates a user to an IMAP4 server and can optionally negotiate a protection mechanism for later protocol interactions.

This RFC describes several mechanisms for that command. Each has an authentication type name: KERBEROS_V4, GSSAPI and SKEY. In every case the server sends 'ready' responses and the client answers, and the exchange ends when the server says OK or NO.
sections.eli5: The mail server asks 'who are you?' in one of three ways, and the program answers in the matching way.

sections.title: Kerberos Version 4 Mechanism
sections.content:
The first ready response carries a random 32-bit number in network byte order. The client replies with a Kerberos ticket and an authenticator for the principal imap.hostname@realm, with the server's number in the encrypted checksum field.

The server checks the checksum, adds one to it, and sends back 8 octets: the incremented checksum, a bit-mask of the protection mechanisms it supports, and the maximum cipher-text buffer size it can receive. These are encrypted in the session key. The client treats the server as authenticated if the first four octets equal one plus the checksum it sent.

The client then sends the original checksum, the bit-mask of the chosen protection, its own maximum buffer size and a user name, padded with one to eight octets to a multiple of eight and PCBC encrypted with the session key. The server verifies it and must check that the principal in the ticket is authorized to connect as that user.

The protection bit-masks are 1 for none, 2 for integrity (krb_mk_safe) and 4 for privacy (krb_mk_priv).
sections.eli5: The server gives the client a random number. The client proves it holds the secret key by sending it back wrapped up, and the server proves itself back by adding one.

sections.title: GSSAPI Mechanism
sections.content:
The type name GSSAPI covers all mechanisms using the Generic Security Service API (RFC 1508). The first ready response has no data. The client calls GSS_Init_sec_context for the target SERVICE:imap@hostname (host name fully qualified and lower case) and sends the resulting token. While the call returns GSS_CONTINUE_NEEDED it keeps exchanging tokens with the server.

When the context is complete, the server sends 4 octets sealed with GSS_Seal: a bit-mask of the protection mechanisms it supports and the maximum message size it can receive. The client replies, also sealed with conf_flag FALSE, with its chosen bit-mask, its own maximum size and a user name. The server must verify that the authenticated source name is authorized to act as that user.

The bit-masks are 1 for no protection, 2 for integrity (sender calls GSS_Seal with conf_flag FALSE) and 4 for privacy (conf_flag TRUE).
sections.eli5: GSSAPI is a standard plug for many security systems. The two sides pass notes back and forth until both are sure, then agree how privately to talk.

sections.title: S/Key One-Time Passwords
sections.content:
The type name for S/Key is SKEY. The first ready response has no data and the client answers with the user name. The second ready response carries a decimal sequence number, a single space and the seed string for that user. The client replies with the one-time password, either as a 64-bit value in network byte order or in the 'six English words' format.

On successful verification the server considers the client authenticated. S/Key does not provide any protection mechanisms. The RFC includes sample logins for success and failure, ending in OK S/Key authentication successful or NO S/Key authentication failed.
sections.eli5: The server asks for the next word on a list of one-use passwords. Each word works only once, so a copied one is useless.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says only that security issues are discussed throughout the memo. The security-relevant points are within the mechanisms themselves: the mutual proof in Kerberos, the integrity and privacy options in Kerberos and GSSAPI, the user authorization checks, and the absence of protection in S/Key.
sections.eli5: The safety rules are built into each handshake rather than listed in one place.

items.label: Integrity
items.desc: Kerberos: krb_mk_safe. GSSAPI: GSS_Seal with conf_flag FALSE.

items.label: Privacy
items.desc: Kerberos: krb_mk_priv. GSSAPI: GSS_Seal with conf_flag TRUE.
